utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in this courtroom and just outside. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. One short procedural matter. D1537 was admitted into evidence although it did not yet appear on the 65 ter list. There was no objection. We have admitted it. It's the excerpt from the Lausic diary. I take it, tendering it, that you intended first to seek leave to add it to your 65 ter list and then to seek admission. But since there is no -- since there was no objection, I don't think that there's any problem with that, although it is not the exact order in which we expect documents to be tendered. Any other procedural matters. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We just wish to inform Court last evening we gave notice to the Defence that we were going to use two additional documents in the examination today, and starting from that there were some discussions, and the parties have reached agreement where the Defence agreed to stipulate to some facts based on which we will not use those documents in the examination, and I wish to record those stipulations into the record. The first one is the Defence stipulates that Witness Boris Milas knew and worked with the Gotovina Defence investigators, Mr. Marin Ivanovic and Vlado Galic within the SIS. The second one is that Luka Misetic, counsel for Ante Gotovina, has visited the premises where witnesses were being proofed by the Defence attorneys in the cases of General Blaskic and Dario Kordic, within the Lora naval base in Split on several occasions at the time the proofings were going on, during 1998 in order to meet with the attorneys for General Blaskic. Stipulation number three is the attorney referred to as Mr. Misetic in the MUP official record of interview of Witness Boris Milas, that is 65 ter 7292, which is yet to be tendered into evidence, is Mr. Luka Misetic, counsel for Ante Gotovina. Stipulation number four, that Mr. Luka Misetic counsel for Ante Gotovina, has no recollection of meeting with Witness Boris Milas prior to 2007 but cannot exclude the possibility that they may have exchanged greetings sometime prior to 2007. Those are the four stipulation, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they are now on the record. The Chamber will consider whether it will invite the parties to formally file this so that it gets the proper attention because, although it's on the record, it might easily be overlooked, but we will consider whether there is need for that. If the parties have any view on it, we'd like to hear; if not, we'll just consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President I have other matters to raise, if I may, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First, furthermore there are discussions going on between the Defence and Prosecution. It is the position of the Gotovina Defence at this point that concerning the allegations that have been put to the witness about documents being hidden from the Prosecution in the Blaskic case that the Prosecution has never alleged before the Appeals Chamber that there was any document that they were seeking that had any material impact on the -- on the Blaskic case that was withheld from them, and there were four Rule 115 motions filed by the Blaskic Defence on appeal. There is no public record of any Rule 115 motion by the Office of the Prosecutor. It also, in a decision, cited yesterday that there were, in fact, five grounds that the Prosecution sought to seek revision of the appeals judgement, none of those five grounds had as a basis that new documents had come to light as a result of concealment. The Prosecution has indicated that the attorneys that worked on the Blaskic case are not currently in The Hague, and, therefore, we will address this matter later with the Chamber after the Prosecution has consulted with their counsel in the Blaskic case about a proposed stipulation to that fact. Second, Mr. President, we wish to at this point -- I don't know want to call it an objection but an observation with a potential objection depending on how things transpire. But at this point, what we have seen through two sessions with this witness is a collateral attack on the witness, on the witness's credibility; and moreover, on the basis of an innuendo that there is some sort of manipulation taking place with the testimony or statement on our part, which obviously we take strong objection to. We wish to cite the Chamber back to a decision that the Chamber gave, and this is at transcript page 2064. It begins at line 8, but it was an oral instruction to Mr. Kehoe during the cross-examination of Mr. Leslie, and I will read it back. "And therefore no problem to deal with the matter" -- and this is now concerning collateral issues on credibility. "But try to do it as efficiently as possible. Come to the point right" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The transcript says, "no ritual bounces as I often say"; I believe, Mr. President, you say no ritual dances: "Let's get to the point right away and let also not forget that this case is not about mistakes or things witnesses have done wrong in the past. Of course, if there are any issues that shed additional light on reliability or credibility, of course, you can deal with the matter but the core of this case is that this Chamber hears evidence about what happened at that time and, of course, also that the Chamber receives relevant information which assists us in assessing credibility and reliability but try to find a balance and do it more quickly." Mr. President, Ms. Mahindaratne has indicated she is going to use four hours of cross-examination. We've used two sessions on collateral matters. I'm not going to object or say that you should impose a time-limit on collateral matters. However I do wish to note at that point we have not addressed any matter concerning 1995. We would ask the Chamber to strike a balance, and, in particular, this collateral attack on the witness is of no value if, in fact, there is nothing that is being disputed in terms of what is in the statement of the witness. Finally, to the extent that the cross-examination by innuendo is allowed, then, Mr. President, we file entitled to go into such matters as Ms. Hartmann's allegations about various intelligence agencies that work inside the Office of the Prosecutor, which she says control the work of the Office of the Prosecutor, et cetera. She is certainly someone who may have been in a position to know these things, whether those intelligence agencies had an impact on this case or not, that is not the type of evidence we thought at this point was relevant to this case. I would agree that if there is something in this witness's testimony that suggests that he has been manipulated, lied, gave false testimony, then it is a relevant area to explore. But in and of itself, the examination thus far, absent that, amounts to the same thing as us starting to read back portions of Ms. Hartmann's book. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. Ms. Mahindaratne, is there any need to respond or do you agree with Mr. Misetic that to find a proper balance is -- as it is always, important.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Absolutely Mr. President. I believe that what I have been doing so far is absolutely legitimate. It was -- there were no innuendos. It was a direct challenge to the credibility of this witness, and I will certainly go into the substance of his testimony. But as one would have seen yesterday, there was a process which delayed my ability to impeach this witness's testimony directly because there was so many objections and interruptions, and I will take only about another five minutes on this subject matter that was discussed yesterday and move on to the substance of his testimony, Mr. President. And I can certainly say I did not make -- there were no innuendos. It was a direct challenge to the credibility of this witness and to demonstrate to the Chamber his bias.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, in defence of myself and other team members, it is innuendo to say that he knows two members of my team and then to explore whether he may have encountered me at some point without any further suggestion of any wrongdoing on anyone's part, particularly in terms of his testimony; and that is why I referred to it as innuendo. I wholeheartedly agree that if there is basis to suggest there is something in his statement that is false or suggested to him as an answer or something to that effect, it is a perfectly legitimate area of cross-examination. I haven't seen it at this point. We've asked whether that was -- there was something specific on that point. We have not received any indication that that is the case. That is why we refer to it as innuendo. You can see by the nature of the stipulations what the innuendo is intended to suggest. Again, I have no problem with it if it is going to be linked directly to something that this witness said in his statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, we'll find out after five minutes. That's what I understand. Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, while the witness is coming, I wonder whether it might be a good time to tender the document which could be tendered yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, a good idea, and that was -- briefly describe the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It was 65 ter 7292, which is the MUP official note of interview with Mr. Boras Milas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will object to that, Your Honour, as I did many times before. This is not an interview that Mr. Milas gave to the police officer. He clearly stated yesterday that the words in that piece of evidence were not his words. Therefore, I think the only proper way to tender this document to the evidence is to have an examination of the police officer who just wrote this document. Otherwise it is no worth of enlisting him -- enlisted this document into the evidence. So this is my strong objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness has gone through the record. He has confirmed that the record is based on his interview. He has confirmed parts of the record, expect for one paragraph. He confirmed that, in fact, the record is based on what he stated to the investigator, and unlike MUP notice coming in without any identification, the person who made the statement is present in court, authenticating and verifying the content, confirming the contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is no in dispute that witness had a conversation with the police officer. What is in dispute is the subject of this conversation as the police officer wrote it down in the Official Note. It is true that witness confirmed that he had a conversation, but this is the only thing. We should go through each and every sentence of this document and ask witness whether he said this and that, and that would be probably the proper way how to proceed with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The exhibit will be MFI'd for the time being. Mr. Registrar the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2548, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning, Mr. Milas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again our apologies that we're busy dealing with other matters and not paying proper attention to your presence. I would like to remind you that the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony still binds you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Milas, it is correct, isn't it, that you have worked with Mr. Marin Ivanovic and Mr. Vlado Galic, the two Defence investigators who interviewed you while you were in the course of your work within the SIS?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marin Ivanovic and Vlado Galic conducted an interview with me in January, February, and May --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And Mr. Milas, please, if you could confine your response to my question. My question is: You have worked with Mr. Marin Ivanovic and Mr. Vlado Galic in the course of your work within the SIS, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, that association, isn't that correct that association with them relates, in part, to your mutual work secreting documents which were required by the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Objective on foundation for the reasons that I stated before. The Prosecution has not responded to my inquiry on that point and -- nor has anything been established in terms of foundation to support that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call, if I'm allowed, Mr. President, I will confront the witness with the document. Mr. Registrar, in the meanwhile, may I call document 7293, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first look at the document to see if there is any foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just add, Mr. President, we had a discussion about this last night, so if that is incorrect, I don't know why I wasn't told of it last night.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may say, the discussion did not relate to this particular documentation. I think Mr. Misetic is fully aware what the discussion was about, and it was very clear that the other documentation which already on the list -- the discussion was with -- related to the additional two documents which were sent last evening. But the other documents which were to be used in this examination were to be -- we were free to proceed with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The confusion is Mr. Waespi and I had a conversation, and I was told that the three -- team were not in town to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Certainly the Chamber has not been present during this conversation. Let's proceed and see what we get on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to make the record clear, Ms. Mahindaratne was present at all times during those phone conversation, so there was nothing exclusive between Mr. Misetic and myself, in relation to this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if I could have that document 7293 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is on the screen, unless there is any other document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If we could just move to page 4 in the English, and Croatian version page 3. I'm sorry before that, Mr. Registrar, my apologies. If you could just go back to page 1; my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, while we go to page 1, Mr. Milas, operation OA Put, as it was known, was also one of the series of operations in place to secrete documents and to prevent evidence from reaching the ICTY; isn't that correct? You are familiar with the term OA Put?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. This is the first time I see this document referring to the OA Put. On the 5th of June, 2000, I told the investigators that I was not familiar with the operative actions, both in terms of the name or what they entailed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You know that this is a record dated 20th September, 1996. It's a document going from Mr. Markica Rebic to the defence minister, Mr. Susak. And it reads, the subject, "Supplement to the work plan for OA Operative Action Put," and it says, "enclosed for your information, please find the supplemental to the work plan for the work of the defence of General Blaskic, et al in the proceedings before the ICTY in The Hague." If you could move now to, Mr. Registrar, to English page 4 and Croatian version page 3. There is it a work plan there. And, Mr. Registrar, if you could focus on the first two cells. The first cell indicates the task as conversation with all the accused, the coordinate is indicated as one of the coordinates is MORH SIS, then letters UN there. And the body in charge is MORH SIS. It says U and the executors are V. Galic, S. Udiljak, and M. Ivanovic. And cell number two reads the task: "Integration and protection of the documentation of the accused staying in the territory of RH." The body in charge MORH SIS, and executor, V. Galic, S. Udiljak, and M. Ivanovic. Now two persons identified there, V. Galic and M. Ivanovic, are Mr. Vlado Galic and Marin Ivanovic who interviewed you in relation to this case; isn't that correct, Mr. Milas?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I tender this document into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to object. The question and the impeachment was: Isn't it true that you participated in secreting documents from this institution through OA Put, with those two gentlemen. Now, first of all, this document doesn't say that. So it is improper impeachment. Second of all, it comes from a date when this witness was not in the SIS, which he has already testified about. So both purposes of the impeachment fail, and I object to the admission of this document as impeachment evidence for a proposition that she hasn't established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the documentation so far discussed and tendered yesterday establishes this witness's connection to the series of operations where the objective was to secret documents from the ICTY proceedings. Now, this document establishes Mr. Galic and Mr. Ivanovic's involvement in the same type of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The wording is, at least, different. Protection of documents may need some further interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I just add one other thing, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In the documents that were tendered into evidence yesterday, Mr. Marinovic -- I'm sorry, Ivanovic's name transpires. It's a logical sequence where, you know, in these documentation, a plan to assist the Defence of General Blaskic, you have Mr. Marin Ivanovic and Mr. Galic's names listed as those protecting documentation relating to the accused. Then, in the documentation that was tendered yesterday, we have this witness's and Mr. Ivanovic names transpiring as people who were responsible for secreting documents, at least concealing documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well transporting documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Transporting document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, choose your words very carefully, Ms. Mahindaratne, and, of course, every party will have its own logic on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr, President, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is it collateral impeachment. This is not direct impeachment on anything he said. Now, I have asked the Office of the Prosecutor over the course of the -- however long we have been in trial, because this issue occasionally pops up, please tell me what documents were ever secreted from you, kept from you; what RFA documents were you seeking that were hidden from you? I never get an answer. So now we're getting this, which is integration and protection of the documentation of the accused. You are to infer means hiding documents from the Office of the Prosecutor, but the Office of the Prosecutor doesn't tie it to any specific RFA. If it is the case then let's get to that document. But this is not the document that established that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This document will be MFI'd. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2549, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just have to tender two more documents, and I will move on to the next subject, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milas, I just am going to ask you just two further questions. Isn't it correct that your department, SIS Split administration, was, in fact, the point of receipt for the documentation that was requested by the ICTY Trial Chamber in the case of General Blaskic from the inception; that was May 1997. Your department was the point of receipt of the documentation. That is my point to you.

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct to the extent that in our department, indeed, documents were brought there, but as to whether those documents were sought by this Honourable Court - that is to say, The Hague Tribunal - I have no knowledge of, for the simple reason that I did not see a single document ever and that I simply didn't know that that may have been someone's intention. Through the Operative Action Haag, I didn't take part in it in terms of knowing or receiving any tasks as well as knowing what the aim of those actions are. As far as the two other operative actions, Put and Istina, as well as the OA Haag, I heard for the first time what they could actually mean on the 5th of June, 2000, when there was the interview I had with the two investigators. I had absolutely no knowledge of the type of documentation, especially not such documentation as would be sought by The Hague Tribunal. Believe me, I did not see a single document from the consignment. I only carried the boxes up to the floor and on the boxes, I could see signs: The 1st brigade, 2nd brigade, travel orders, or some such things. I had been with the army for a number of years. Therefore, I could logically conclude that these documents had to do with the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me show you two document, Mr. Milas, and I will move on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I have document 7295, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Milas, we will see a document on the screen, which is, in fact, a receipt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you asked the previous one to be under seal. If we now continue in open session to deal with the document, although in a different way, would that affect in any way what you asked us two minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I don't see any indications on this particular document, you know, a direct reference to the contents of the previous document. This is a quite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. 7295. I'm sorry, 7294.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Milas, that's the record, receipt of taking over archives issued on 22nd May, 1997 at the Lora naval base, and it lists out an entire number of archives. Of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If would you first wait until the question has been formulated. If you then want to comment on the question or point at any accuracy in the question, you are free to do so. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I only wanted to ask for the document to be enlarged so that I could see it better. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This, in fact, reflects, Mr. Milas, that on 22nd May, 1997, your chief, Mr. Mario Tomasovic, received, on behalf of the Lora base and your department, an entire list of archives of documents relating to HVO and many Military Districts. Do you see that document? Perhaps you might want to go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the document. Could I see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think in the Croatian version it is only one page. You can see who has signed and the seals?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that the document was signed by Major Miroslav Klepic. I suppose he is a member of the HVO, and I can see that nobody signed the document on behalf of the Lora base. We only see the name of Mario Tomasovic written in -- by hand, but his signature is not there. This is not his signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: But this document, in fact, reflects that these archives of documentation were received at the Lora base in May 1997 at a time, in fact, you were serving in that department. Does it not?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This record speaks of the contents of the HVO documentation handed over at Lora. You asked me if it was signed. I can see that it is not, but its contents indicate that this would have to do with the HVO documentation. Thus, indirectly, one could conclude that it has to do with that sort of documentation. However, I have never seen this document before, and I don't know that the chief of the department, Mario Tomasovic, would sign such a document, primarily because had he actually signed the document, the seal of the Croatian army or the Ministry of Defence would have had to be attached to it. From what I can see, we only have the seal of the Ministry of Defence Mostar, the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Bosnia and Herzegovina. Again, this is the first time I see the document. Now, whether it relates to the document that we, indeed, archived at the Lora facility, that's something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The document will be MFI'd, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I may also, Mr. President, for the record, I'm not sure that I'm reading the subpoena and comparing it to the documents, so I'm not sure that the documents sought actually are in the documents identified in this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I can't get the subpoena right away on my screen. I was -- I did write down for myself to compare at least to start with the dates and then to have a closer look at the subpoena. 24 Dates, subpoena was dated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: 30 April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I belive it's 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Subpoena was dated 30th April, 1997, Mr. President, with a order to report by 27th May, 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a closer look. If you want to further explain your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because we we've now gone two hours plus into this topic. Whether the Chamber now wants the Defence to start introducing evidence about what archives were hidden, at what location, whether they were subject of a subpoena, et cetera, we will be glad to do that. In the alternative, I would suggest that the Office of the Prosecutor advise the Chamber whether any of the documents sought, in fact, were kept from the Office of the Prosecutor in the Blaskic case, to cut this story short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, as I said before, the document will be MFI'd. Let me try to understand what happens at this moment. It seems Ms. Mahindaratne seeks to establish that the involvement of the SIS in the preparation of the Blaskic Defence at the time, and the -- went beyond what is usually the association between government authorities and the defence of private individuals; whereas, we heard from the witness that he explains the documentation you've shown as a neutral activity in transporting documents without any knowledge of why these documents had to be transported and by providing space, transportation to potential witnesses, and providing them with coffee or other drinks at the time. So, therefore, that apparently is the issue where Ms. Mahindaratne seeks to establish certain matters. There is -- there are suggestions which are vehemently challenged by the Defence. That is, that the documents in itself allow for any further conclusions than what the witness said. That, apparently, is the issue at this moment. What you suggest becomes clear from the way in which you are phrasing your questions. Protecting documents is interpreted in a certain way by you; whereas, other interpretations of what these documents say are given by the witness, and the issue of interpretation of these documents, I think the Defence urges the Chamber to stick as closely to the text as one could do. I think I've, more or less, summarized what we've heard. Ms. Mahindaratne, six time five minutes is half an hour. Could you move on to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have concluded with that section. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document on the screen should be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will become Exhibit P2551, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Milas, now, in your statement you describe regular tasks of the military police and extraordinary tasks. Now this may be an obvious question, but isn't that correct that the principal function, or should I say the main function of the criminal military police, is crime prevention and crime processing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crime prevention service of the military police performs the duties which, under the Law on Criminal Procedure, are normally carried out by members of the MUP but only in relation to the crimes which fall within the jurisdiction of the military court; in other words, crimes committed by military personnel, crimes committed by citizens employed in the service of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, and which offences had to do with the performance of their duties and for other criminal offences which such civilians or other such citizens commit together with the military personnel. Furthermore, the crime prevention service also processes the offences committed by civilians but only in respect of those offences which were, at the time exhaustively listed in the rules governing the work of the units of the armed forces in Article 54 and which relate to certain sections or chapters -- or, rather, certain, chapters or sections of the crimes listed in the Criminal Code valid or in force at the time. That's, in short, the duties the crime prevention service or criminal investigation military police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, that -- in order to reach -- carry out that function, that would entail tasks such as identification and arrest of perpetrators, search of premises, search for suspects and evidence, carrying out forensic investigations, processing of criminal reports or charges, producing suspects or accused before judicial bodies; isn't that correct what I just read out? These are the regular tasks of the crime prevention section of the military police, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the better part of what you mentioned, that's correct. On the issue of searches, the crime investigation military police will issue an order, a warrant to that effect, when it has to do with documentation or individuals, and this will be carried out or the -- such a warrant for search will be acted upon by the search personnel of the 72nd Battalion. The -- in other words, they would deal with all those criminal investigations and processing which fall under the jurisdiction of the military court in respect of those who are suspected of having committed crimes that fall also within the territorial -- or, rather --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, that fall within the subject matter jurisdiction of military courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, maintaining check-points and conducting military police patrols, which part of the military police was responsible? The crime prevention section or the general military police of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such tasks, based on a previously worked out plan, were performed by members of the general police force. However, depending on the personnel available, members of the crime investigation military police would also sometimes man check-points. However, I'm not aware of many such situations having transpired.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And manning check-points and conducting military police patrols was part of the regular tasks of the general military police; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And isn't it correct that one of the objectives of maintaining check-points and conducting military police was the detection and -- of crime, detection of perpetrators; for example, at check-points people who were looting goods would be stopped and detected and arrested, and patrols would arrest perpetrators of crime? Isn't that one of the objectives of check-points and patrols?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, it was the duty of those manning check-points to do precisely what you said, but not only that. They would also control the movement of persons going in or out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether that was one of the objectives which already includes that there may have been others. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milas, you discuss the rules governing the structure and operation of the military police of the armed forces. In your statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have P880, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in your statement, you go through an interpretation of how you understand the -- how we understand Article 8 and 9 and 10 to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if you could go on to, Mr. Registrar, page 6 of the English version, and perhaps page -- the relevant page would be, in the Croatian version -- yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, the tasks that we just discussed as regular tasks, are enumerated in item 2 of Article 10, isn't that correct, prevention and uncovering of crimes, identification and arrest of perpetrators of crimes that fall within the jurisdiction of military judicial bodies, operative and forensic investigation, and escorting the perpetrator of these crimes to appear before the bodies in charge. Isn't it correct that the tasks that we just discussed is caught up in item 2?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 2 refers to the tasks of the one of the services; namely, the crime prevention service.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And now if you go back to page 1, the previous page, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Milas, the language in Article 9 is this: "While performing their regular military police tasks, military police units are subordinate to the commander of the Military District, the commander of the HRM" -- there are many other entities mentioned but we are interested in the first description. So the regular tasks, now we agreed here in court what they were. So when the military police carries out those tasks under this Article, they're subordinated to the Military District Commander; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tasks of the crime investigation military police are performed solely ex officio on the request of a military prosecutor or that of a military court. Not a single -- no order is necessary for members of the crime investigation military police to act. They are bound to act by the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is correct. But isn't it right that, based on what we agreed, now we have agreed what the regular military police tasks of the crime section was, we have agreed that maintaining check-points and conducting patrols were regular tasks of the general military police. Now on the face of this language, isn't it right that in the course of these -- carrying out those regular tasks, the military police was subordinated to the Military District Commander?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is one thing to erect check-points, and the tasks listed under item two that we've just looked at are a different matter altogether because they relate to the duties of only the crime prevention service; whereas the manning of check-points falls under the duties of the general duty military police. The two should not be confused.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's not debate on this, Mr. Milas. Let me take you to Article 16 of this, and that would be at page 13 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it would be easier for the witness, I hard copy of the statements if you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, that seems to be a good idea, that hard copies will be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm just asking to go to -- not the statement, Mr. Milas, Article 16 of this on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And that would be, Mr. Registrar, page 13 of the English version. I think on the Croatian, we are on the correct page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can the font be enlarged, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Does this assist you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] It's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milas, do you see Article 16? And, in fact, I think there is a typographical error in the second paragraph. We'll go with the first paragraph, Article 16. It says: "The military police shall carry out the tasks listed in these rules through the following services: Security, search, patrol, escort, duty, military traffic, safety, and crime prevention." And the next paragraph reads this: "The members of the military police carry out the tasks and jobs of the services under paragraph 1," that is the first paragraph we just read, "ex officio on orders of the senior commander of the military police, on orders by the senior HV commander from," and this reads Article 7, but it should be, I think the Defence will agree, Article 9 because Article 7 relates to a completely irrelevant subject, "Article 9 of the rules and requests from the body in charge, they carry out specific jobs and tasks pursuant to an order issued by the senior commander of the military police unit or the duty officer in the military police duty service." So do you see, Mr. Milas, this Article 16 provides that military police carries out the -- their tasks which have to be carried out through those services enumerated in paragraph 1, pursuant to an order from the commander of the military police or, an order by the senior HV commander, or an authorised -- I'm sorry, or body in charge. So isn't it correct that amongst the -- the entities mentioned there, the Military District Commander would also be authorised to issue orders to the military police to carry out the tasks through the services mentioned in paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] para 2 of Article 16 speaks of what I have mentioned a minute ago, among other things, tasks are performed ex officio, then following an order of a superior commander of the military police, and upon receiving an order of a superior officer. The distinction is made in the sense that part of the tasks falling exclusively within the remit of the military crime police are done ex officio. Performing tasks of that nature falls under the category of ex officio. As for the tasks in Article 10, with ten items specified therein, it is stated there that tasks are performed following an order of a superior military police officer. If you look into the rules of service of the military police, you will see that a superior officer of the Croatian army, within a given territory, has the right to issue orders to the military police. There is a distinction between the tasks ex officio and then following an order of a superior commander and following an order of a superior army officer. If you analyse the role of the military police stipulated in paragraph 1 of Article 16, you realize that some of such services can, following a request of a superior commander, can implement certain tasks. But when it says ex officio in para 2 of Article 10 of the rules, mention is made of the crime military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milas, isn't it correct that your immediate commander was Colonel Budimir?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Budimir, commander of the 72nd MP Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And isn't it right that you received your orders from Colonel Budimir for your daily tasks, regular tasks?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military orders pertaining exclusively to the military component of the work of the military police, in that case, yes. As for the prevention of crime, we received separate orders along our professional chain of command, along which we also reported. When Mr. Budimir issued orders, he didn't issue separate orders to the crime prevention service in a way that it would be duty-bound to process a crime, or that it was duty-bound to find the perpetrator. We were duty-bound to do that ex officio.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. But what type of orders did General -- Colonel Budimir issue to you?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Budimir never issued a separate order to the crime prevention service. The crime prevention service, or, rather, its employees, were duty-bound to act upon an order of the commander when he issued an order that would include all segments of work of the military police and need to be performed by, say, the 1st of December, and they should forward their reports on activities undertake so that he, as the commander, could draft an annual report and submit it to General Lausic. If the 72nd Battalion participated in the implementation of an action, such as the RAIS actions that loosely translate as order and discipline, such operations following orders of Colonel Budimir would have to do with all segments of the work of the military police and its component, the military crime police, in the course of implementation of such actions. In the sense of issuing an order pertaining to an individual offence or a group of offences, we never received such an order from the commander of the 72nd Battalion for processing. We received certain professional instruction and orders by the department of the crime military police within the administration of the military police. As soldiers, irrespective of the fact that we were employees of the crime prevention service, we were duty-bound to abide by the military order in the sense of arriving at the barracks --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Milas, is it possible for you to keep your responses, you know, brief, simply because of the time constraints. So, you know, but all means say what you have to say but as briefly as possible. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, putting focussed questions to the witness will certainly assist in achieving the goal you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President I will try --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have to apologise. I just try to assist you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milas, isn't it correct -- I'm not referring to specific orders by General -- by Colonel Budimir saying, Go and process that crime, in that sense. But isn't it correct that Colonel Budimir issued you orders relating to maintenance of law and order, you know, general orders in the crime section. You're in charge of crime detection and processing in this particular area, in that type, orders relating to the maintenance of law and order. If you could answer with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not possible to say yes or no. He issued orders but never in a way so as to specify separate tasks of the crime prevention service.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Milas, I did in fact qualify it. I said -- I'm in the relating to specific tasks. Did Colonel Budimir issue orders generally, general orders in relation to maintenance of law and order in the territory that came within your area of responsibility? I'm not relating to specific tasks but general orders relating to maintenance of law and order?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: General orders, yes; but not in respect of the crime prevention service, as such. For example, stepping up patrolling measures, asking for IDs and bringing in people who did not abide by the military discipline. Or, rather, in certain cases when the security alertness had to be raised, all that fell within the remit of the military police in terms of their powers and authority and the use of is what he could cover in his orders, such as checking up check-point, the beat service, patrol service in certain areas, checking IDs; but in such orders, it was not explicitly stated that some tasks should be performed by the crime prevention service as such. It is a normal thing that if a military patrol comes across a person breaching military discipline or in the course of committing a crime, then they would notify the crime prevention service that was duty-bound to act upon that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, isn't it correct that you reported to Colonel Budimir on a daily basis both orally and in writing?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and I said so in the same time, not in writing, though. It was done in the course of the morning briefings. In written form, it was only when submitting monthly, semi-annual or annual reports or if the chief of administration of the military police asked Commander Budimir for a report on a certain event, then I, as the chief of the crime prevention service, would draft that, and Colonel Budimir would forward it to General Lausic. We report to the commander in writing only by virtue of those monthly, semi-annual an annual reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: However, isn't it correct that you reported to the duty service of the battalion on a daily basis. The reports of your section went to the duty service of the battalion, 72nd Battalion, on a daily basis. There were daily reports.

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty service would be notified orally on the measures we undertook when we would be notified by the duty service that we should act, after having done so, we would report to them orally. They would include the actions taken by us in their daily report that they forwarded to various addressees.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, those reports that you gave to the duty service included reports on the work of the crime service section, about processing -- processes of crime or arrest, or whatever action the crime service department has taken for the day; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: An officer tasked with processing a certain crime would advise orally the duty officer at the duty office on the measures taken following their notification of a crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And that fact would be recorded in the -- the duty service log; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be recorded in the daily report of the duty service of the 72nd Battalion, which was daily sent to several addressees.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And among the several addressees was -- one report went to the Military District commander; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know that Colonel Budimir had daily briefings with General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they met daily, and I have my doubts about that, but he did probably participate in certain meetings when invited by the Military District Commander, although I don't think it was on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we briefly discuss the further order of today's hearing, but I'd like to already invite Madam Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. We have a break of approximately half an hour, Mr. Milas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, what you announced to be five minutes was half an hour; therefore, I have some concerns. Could you give us an indication as to how much further time you would need.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I believe about two and a half hours, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Or perhaps I try to keep it in two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, the Chamber has, as always, monitored the way in which the cross-examination was conducted. The Chamber is not unaware of some interruptions and some obstacles you met during you cross-examination; nevertheless, the Chamber encourages you very much to finish your cross-examination in the next session, which would be a hour and a half. If you will not be able to do that, the Chamber will then consider looking at how you used your time in that one session, whether or not it will allow you any further time. And as a general guidance, if you start your question by saying it is an obvious question and then ask for a -- seeking long answers which takes up a couple of minute, where one could have imagined that you would have immediately put the next question and leaving out the obvious question, but these are just -- try to keep your cross-examination focussed. And, again, long answers are often the result of not focussed questions. We'll have a break, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milas, I ask you to -- to give focussed answers on what Ms. Mahindaratne asks you, yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milas, just before the break you said that you were not certain if, in fact, Mr. Budimir had daily meetings with General Gotovina. Let me tell you this Trial Chamber has heard evidence. The commander of the Knin military police, Mr. Bosko Dzolic testified. And his testimony is at P875, paragraph 15 and P876, paragraph 6. And he testified that Colonel Budimir in fact met with General Gotovina for daily briefings. And that these meetings were conducted for Colonel Budimir to give a report on the ground situation to General Gotovina. Now, your testimony is that apart from -- let me also inform you the Split Military District operations diary, P17 has been tendered into evidence which records working meetings conducted by General Gotovina at which a representative of the military police battalion is recorded as attending those working meetings, and there are discussions recorded. Now, your testimony is that General Gotovina did not issue a direct order to you on crime prevention. Isn't it correct that, in fact, General Gotovina did not have to issue you direct orders. His orders were conveyed to you via Colonel Budimir?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that we performed our duties ex officio, which did not require the issuing of any orders, including, those of the commander of the 72nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, are you aware that General Gotovina, in fact, did issue orders to Colonel Budimir, to maintain law and order during and in the aftermath of Operation Storm? Do you know that, in fact, General Gotovina did issue such orders to Colonel Budimir?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, myself, am not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me, in fact, show you what Colonel Budimir says about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May have I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, one of the things that I'm asking myself is this witness testified that there may have been meetings, but he has some doubt on whether these were daily meetings or not. We do not have to convince this witness. If he says, I do not know whether Mr. Budimir obtained such orders which means can be the case, cannot be the case. Apparently, that is at least how I understand his answer, that could have been a focussed question: When Mr. Budimir gave you any orders, did he ever tell you that he was passing orders that came from General Gotovina? Because that is a factual question. If the witness does not know, then he doesn't know. And we don't have to convince him of the truthfulness of what others testified in this Court. So, of course, I do not know what -- what direction you will go, but up until now, I -- I got the impression that where the witness says he doesn't know, that you want to convince him through documents put to him that what he doesn't know might well be A, B, or C which is, of course, not the purpose for which the witness is here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President it is that his testimony and statements are -- where he says that, in fact, General Gotovina was not involved in issuing orders relating to crime prevention. I was going to only address that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He also said that during these meetings, do but please proceed, you are aware what is worrying me a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, I hear you, Mr. President. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milas, yesterday you testified that Major Juric was in fact -- was considered a commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion. Isn't it correct that Major Juric was withdrawn on the 14th of August?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether Major Juric was removed on the 4th of August, I don't know that. On the 4th of August --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Milas, I said 14th of August he was withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was interpreted to me as the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This has now been corrected. Was he withdrawn on the 14th of August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To my knowledge, Mr. Juric was not removed. He was simply dispatched back to his earlier duties, back to Zagreb, together with the other members of the team, who had accompanied him initially.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And isn't it correct, Mr. Milas, that Major Juric and Ante Glavan and the other person you referred to was sent down from the military police administration to coordinate activities, to assist with the military police tasks and not to command the 72nd Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: General's order of the 2nd of August, 1995 is quite clear. I believe that in item one the order clearly states that they will -- he will be in command of the 72nd MP Battalion and elements of the 73rd MP Battalion attached to the 72nd, and they will take part in the performance of all the policing duties. In military terms, the task issued was -- issued very clearly, where an order states that an individual is superior to another individual, then he is, in fact, his commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, page 38, line 9 from what I heard from the original, the witness started saying General Lausic's order. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you testified in your statement you say that Major Juric was introduced to you at a meeting by Colonel Budimir. Now, in fact, let me show you what -- how Colonel Budimir understood Major Juric's role to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if could I call 65 ter 7288, please. And if you could go to paragraph 17, that would be on the English page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You see --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour as a practice, I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As a practice, I am concerned about statements of a non-witness not called by the Prosecutor being put to a witness as a way of asserting the truth. And in my submission, that is not a practice that should be accepted by the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Defence has, you know, followed this practice throughout the course of the Prosecution's phase of the case, where witnesses who testify on a particular position is confronted with a contradictory question given by another witness, particularly one -- another witness who, in this case, this is this witness's commander who introduced this witness to Major Juric. So there is certainly a basis to confront this witness with what Colonel Budimir has stated on this. And this is a practice that has been followed by the Defence throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can reply to that. First of all, Prosecution have called their evidence, put their case. Attempt to go use material in this way that is unchallenged by the Defence in any form of cross-examination, analysis with the witness, and asserting it as the truth to this witness, in my submission that is absolutely contradictory to the principles of admissibility of evidence. One can see as a device and tactical that it is -- undermines the principle of the reception of evidence into a trial. My learned friend justifies the use of the material by saying, Well it's the contradictory position of the witness in a statement. We don't know that. They never called the witness to support that. They never -- it is a record of a statement taken by someone else. We don't know in what circumstances. We don't know whether it would be adopted or accepted. And the Defence would not be able to question the maker of it. In my submission, the cross-examination should take this form: That my learned friend asks this witness questions about what he knows and about what he saw, and does not put statements made by others whom we don't know whether they are correct or not. It doesn't help this witness as to his own position to be told, Well, another person in another statement said this about the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is it your intention to later then tender this statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I wish to merely confront this witness with a contradictory question and see if he would reconsider his testimony. And I have already, in fact, questioned this witness on this particular position and obtained his answer and once that is done there is a practice, in fact, in this process where we followed it. Where once a question is asked from a witness, obtains an answer, and then the contradictory question is placed before from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If my recollection is correct, we often said to the Defence, if you want to use a certain statement then wait until you have called that witness. I remember that we MFI'd several times statements in respect of this. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, there are ways of achieving your aim without using this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, you can lead the witness if you would --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know whether I made myself clear. I don't intend to tender the statement at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't intend to tender the statement, then there are other means of --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's not do it on the basis of this statement, which doesn't mean that you cannot ask questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milas, do you know that, in fact, Mr. Budimir has described the role of Major Juric as that of a coordinator and not a commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, and, in fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, now I would, unfortunately, have to dispute the way that that was characterized, the second portion of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now we have a problem, Mr. Misetic, because I invited Ms. Mahindaratne --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to do it in the way she wants to do it. Now whether it mischaracterizes or not, the statement is apparently --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just described as not a commander is the portion that I'm concerned about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well. I'll strike out that last bit and just rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I can just -- because the way the question was answered -- asked sums up the problem. This witness has attempted to be persuaded, as Your Honour used the phrase before the break, I think spotting a potential problem there, by being told what someone else has said and will you change your recollection and evidence. And it -- I think that that is a very danger practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see the point. Let try to cut matters short.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milas, it transpires that Ms. Mahindaratne received information from Mr. Budimir that he saw the role of Mr. Juric rather in the -- as a coordinating role. In practice, so apart from what the formal position was as being a commander, would you agree that his role was primarily a coordinating role, rather than commanding in any day-to-day work or operational work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I was present at the meeting of the 3rd of August in the evening, to my mind, the relationship was quite clear. Major Juric was the superior to the commander of the 72nd Battalion, and he had the duty to coordinate with commanders of Military Districts, the most senior officers in the area and chiefs of police administrations. This is what the order by General Lausic states, and this is what, at this meeting at 2300 hours on the 3rd of August was said to all those who were present, including Major Juric, Ante Glavan, and Mr. Cicvaric from the administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Milas, I'm not contesting the fact that Major Juric may have been, by function, superior, when he sent down [sic]. But it is your terminology that he was a commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion that I tried to, you know, contest by letting you know what how Colonel Budimir described his --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very concerned. My learned friend is giving evidence. One of the important criteria for cross-examination is that questions are asked, the witness is being attempted to be influenced by showing her knowledge from some other -- which may be wrong, and it can mislead the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, there is no reason to explain to a witness what you are contesting or what are you not contesting. Put questions to the witness, and the witness has now told us twice that he was appointed in a commanding position but that he was tasked with coordinating functions as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you know Brigadier Biskic, don't you, Mr. Milas, you have worked with him.

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: He was a deputy to General Lausic in the military police administration; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In fact, Brigadier Biskic, himself, described --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm trying to impeach the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let, let's, let's ... let's instruct the witness not to answer a question. You said, "In fact, Brigadier Biskic himself described." Where did he do that, did he --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In his statement, Mr. President, to the OTP, and generally if we were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But what applies for the previous statement applies here as well. Please phrase your question in such a way that it will not meet objections. I think I gave you guidance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, with respect may I say I'm unable to understand where the Defence were allowed to, in fact, cross-examine in this manner, you know, confront witnesses with statements made by person who had not, in fact, been called to testify. In fact, OTP statements were confronted -- were read back to witnesses and confronted with the contradictory position and their views obtained. Now we are merely following a practice that has been followed in these proceedings for the last one year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One major difference certainly is, Ms. Mahindaratne, that during the Prosecution's case when there is not yet a witness list for the Defence that matters are still open; whereas, here, the Prosecution has presented its case. Let me consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just say briefly, if I wasn't clear, I'm not trying to introduce the content, substance of this statement into the record, I'm merely confronting the witness with the content --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- for impeachment purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, you tell the witness what someone said, and as Mr. Kay said before, that would still be a matter to be established rather than to be a fact and that, of course, may have been one of the reasons why he went on his feet. Because you said for a fact, this is what he said. Now, of course, there are ways of phrasing such a question, where it is not presented as fact, but where you, nevertheless, can ask the witness something about what some person may have said to the Prosecution. If I would tell you that someone told this, what would be your answer to such a suggestion, which is different from, This person said this and this and this, does that refresh your memory? So there are ways of dealing with the matter in such a technical way, Ms. Mahindaratne, I think that you would not be interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Milas, what -- I inform you that the Prosecution is in possession of information --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am very concerned, because this is -- just put the question. Just -- just whatever the information is whatever, whatever it is, just ask the witness the question and allow him to deal with it. I'm very concerned about procedure that seems to suborn a witness on the basis of alleged or apparent information the Prosecution may have about facts, which is, for them, nothing to do with this witness, and attempting to suborn the witness in that way, in my submission, we are not hearing the witness's evidence, we are hearing something else. It is much better, just put the question, I put to you, I -- this daily meetings happened, or, I put to you, meetings happened once a week, and put your case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have asked that question, now the witness has given an answer. Now the Prosecution has the right, the cross-examining party has right, to confront the witness with contradictory information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's start --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I say one thing, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Very briefly. It is our position that the Prosecution, in cross-examination, should put its case to the witness using whatever has been admitted as part of its case thus far or whatever it will seek to admit in the course of cross-examination to a witness, but put matters to a witness that will not be part of the Prosecution case, we believe is improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, Rule 90(H) gives you an obligation that if the witness contradicts what apparently is the Prosecution's case in a certain respect that you put your case to him. Is that -- not by saying that another witness said that, but by saying that the Prosecution takes the position that, this and this and this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did that. My first question to him was, Wasn't it correct that Major Juric, Ante Glavan, and other person were sent in by the administration as coordinators, and thereafter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: His answer apparently contradicted what your case was. So then the next step is -- it is the Prosecution's case that you are not giving the right answer because it's the Prosecution case that this and this and this happened. There is no need at this moment then to refer to statements which other persons have given. So put your case to the witness. I do agree that's your obligation under Rule 90(H), and that only appears once you start by putting a leading question to the witness, and when he then, in his answer, denies the correctness of what you have suggested to him. Therefore, if he contradicts the Prosecution's case in his answer, then you should put your case to him and say, It's the Prosecution's position that this answer is wrong because we think this and this, and or we have established or we try to establish that this and this is the case. That's what Rule 90(H) requires you to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President beyond that, if the witness still contradicts, am I allowed to then confront him with evidence from other sources, or not evidence but information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I corrected myself, Mr. President, information from other sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether you say it, or whether Mr. X says or Mr. Y says it, or Mr. Z says so, if the Defence has not had an opportunity to cross-examine the witness, then your position isn't any different -- apart from that you have to prove your case, isn't any different from what A, B, C, or X, Y or Z telling us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Milas, I put it to you that Major Juric, Ante Glavan, and the third person you mentioned were sent down from the military police administration as coordinators to assist in the military police activity and not as commanders, not to command the 72nd Military Police Battalion. How do you respond to that? And if could you be brief with your response.

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Lausic's order is clear: If I, as a soldier, spoke about coordination, whereas it is clear that they were superior, would be irresponsible of me. General Lausic -- had General Lausic wanted to appoint Mr. Juric coordinator, he would have noted down in his order. Based on our experience from Operation Flash, General Lausic, for that reason, drafted the order in such a way that Mr. Juric was superior to the commander of the 72nd Battalion. If he had wanted him to act as coordinator, he would have put that in. In the order, he stated that, among other things, he also coordinates work with the commanders in the area -- in the district area with brigade commanders and chiefs of police administrations. General Lausic was clear in his order. This is how I see the order and the situation surrounding it. As for who said what and who had what interpretation and impressions, that is not up to me. I see that you have some other information or statements, but you should put such questions to the persons who interpreted the situation that way. I cannot offer a comment on someone else's statement. I can tell you about what I know, because, at 2300 hours on the 3rd of August, I was at the forward command post in Sajkovici when those officers from the administration came and when the order was read out to us. I have no other impression of that event.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
